source.title: Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision
source.authors: Dor Tirosh; Ido Amos; Mor Geva

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a student can succeed where a weaker teacher fails, but uses teacher-forced state distributions during training rather than fine-tuning a pretrained student on the teacher’s task labels.
record.gate_note: The S5 state-tracking experiment directly compares a student trained with a task-failing Transformer teacher against that teacher. The language-modeling benchmark gains and method ablations are not rows: they do not compare performance against a weaker task supervisor. The paper does not report PGR.
record.test_reason: The S5 student is not trained only on a weaker supervisor's labels. Per §B.1, the teacher-fed LIFT models keep the gold answer loss and add a KL term to the teacher plus the teacher's states as inputs. The Transformer×8 'teacher' is trained on the same gold labels. The student-beats-teacher gap therefore reflects LIFT's feedback architecture, which the paper attributes to expressivity, rather than generalisation from weak supervision. No weak-label-only training, strong ceiling or PGR exists. Burns et al. is cited only in related work as an analogy ('the student can surpass its teacher').
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that a teacher-forced latent feedback channel lets a fixed-depth LIFT solve S5 lengths its same-depth Transformer teacher cannot, though without unbounded depth: it fails beyond the training range. They also conclude that LIFT LMs from 135M to 1B beat token- and compute-matched Transformers. The framing is architectural expressivity and efficient parallel pretraining, not weak-to-strong generalisation.
record.recipe_differences: The student is trained from scratch with teacher-forced output-distribution states as inputs and supervision, alongside task/token losses; it is not a pretrained strong model fine-tuned on weak task labels, and PGR is not calculated.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with S5 sequence length: the student reaches 100% at N=12 and solves half the sequences at N=16; the Transformer teacher is at chance at these lengths.

fits_no_version.finding: On S5 at N=12, a two-layer LIFT trained with gold answer loss plus a failing same-depth Transformer's states and KL reaches 100%, while the teacher is near chance. At 1B, LIFT pretrained with gold next-token loss plus teacher states beats its 2×-token teacher on arithmetic BPB.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A student given gold supervision plus a weaker teacher's soft states as inputs can exceed that teacher when its architecture is more expressive (teacher-as-input surpassing, not weak-to-strong).

record.problems: The weak-teacher comparison is a synthetic S5 experiment at one fixed model size and architecture. The student is trained from scratch, not fine-tuned from a strong pretrained checkpoint; PGR and numerical uncertainty for the cited length-specific results are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. Pretrained-LM benchmark comparisons and LIFT ablations do not compare a student’s task performance against a weak task supervisor.

untested.parts: No strong model is trained on weak labels alone; gold task loss is always present; no PGR or strong ceiling.
Not tested; teacher strength in §D.4 concerns LM perplexity with gold next-token loss, not weak supervision.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's relation 'tests'/T2 and all V1/V3 labels are removed. §B.1 states that teacher-fed models 'add the forward KL' to the existing losses, so gold answers supervise the student. The teacher is also the gold-trained baseline. The weak-to-strong framing appears only in the §G analogy.

versions.untested_parts: Tests teacher-supervised learning on a synthetic state-tracking task, not fine-tuning a strong pretrained model on weak task labels; no PGR is reported.
The study does not test auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, or whether those changes raise PGR over naive weak-label fine-tuning.
Tests one synthetic task and a fixed two-layer, same-size teacher/student setup; does not sweep model sizes or test NLP, chess, reward modelling, or predictors of PGR.
Does not test supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift, or error overlap as failure modes of weak-label fine-tuning.
Does not test theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.

rows.subject: Transformer×8
rows.uncertainty: Standard error over 3 seeds is reported for the figure; numerical error not stated for this result.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as the teacher for the corresponding LIFT model; the abstract reports 3% at N=12.
rows.check: The teacher was trained on gold labels, so this is not a weak supervisor in the V1 sense. It also has a value discrepancy: the abstract and §1 give 3% at N=12, but §C.1 says the Transformer stays at ≈10% at N=12 across budgets.

rows.check: The student is trained with the gold answer loss plus teacher states and KL, not on weak labels alone. The gain over the teacher shows LIFT's architectural advantage, not weak-to-strong generalisation.
